title: BBC Gardeners’ World Live
excerpt: Morgan Oates was selected as one of five APL Avenue Show Gardens at BBC Gardeners’ World Live 2019.
body: Morgan Oates was selected as one of five APL Avenue Show Gardens at BBC Gardeners’ World Live 2019 in Birmingham. Entrants were asked to design a space inspired by other countries and cultures.

Designer Anna Pawlowska set out to create a retreat where clients could leave work and daily worries behind. Drawing on Moroccan culture, she designed a sensory garden built around sound, scent, views and texture.

A central island resembles a wild meadow, with a bench among fragrant, pollinator-friendly flowers in calming colours. A shallow pool of clear blue water surrounds it, so visitors can cool their feet after a long, hot day, and patterned Moroccan-style tiles make a dry path around the water.

Tall, flowing grasses line the borders for year-round interest and a gentle sound in the wind. A large sculpture behind the bench is the focal point, framed by star jasmine and an ornamental cherry. Off-white fencing keeps the garden bright through the year, and a decked area at the entrance, with a bistro set, looks across the whole garden.

title: Christmas Decorations
review: Seasonal; traditions described as the original author wrote them.
excerpt: Where the Christmas decoration tradition came from, and a traditional palette of green, red and holly.
body: Christmas decorations began as a way of marking the birth of Jesus, with homes dressed in red and green on Christmas Eve. Today people decorate much earlier, use a wider range of colours and often choose longer-lasting artificial materials.

For a traditional look the article suggests green, for the continuity of life; red, recalling Jesus’s blood at the Crucifixion; and holly, whose spiky leaves stand for the crown of thorns and whose red berries stand for drops of blood.
By tradition, decorations went up on 24 December and came down before 5 January, since leaving them longer was said to bring bad luck.

title: Japanese Gardens
review: General background; the history is the original author’s summary and has not been fact-checked.
excerpt: What most Japanese gardens share: rock, water, evergreens, maples and the idea of nature in miniature.
body: Japanese gardens reflect a deep love of landscape. Their designs draw on the country’s native greenery and on older Chinese garden traditions, while staying close to everyday life. The earliest records date from the Suiko period (552–645), and eight distinct styles are now recognised.

Most share a handful of features: natural rock and stone paving, some of it practical, such as a basin for washing; ponds with jets or fountains; islands, cascades, bridges and hills; and plenty of greenery.

Evergreens dominate and pine is the most prized, standing for longevity. Maples are the favourite deciduous tree, alongside cherry, magnolia, camellia, wisteria and hydrangea, with irises, lilies, asters and anemones beneath.
A central principle is nature in miniature: trees and shrubs are pruned with great care so that they look natural and picturesque, as they would in the wild.

title: Choosing a Garden Designer
review: Opinion piece. The author promised a follow-up on later design stages that was never published.
excerpt: Why it is hard to find the right designer, and what the first site meeting should cover.
body: It is not easy to find the right garden designer, because many courses and diplomas allow people to use the title. A good designer needs wide knowledge: garden and architectural history, horticulture, climate and geography, topography and geology, art and garden styles, safety, construction and legal restrictions. Formal training matters, but hands-on experience matters more.
The article argues that a local designer is generally more dependable than one working from another country, because local plants, soils and weather vary so much.
Garden design is a staged process. Its core task is organising space into outdoor rooms for recreation, dining or play, which, being made of plants, change with the seasons.
The designer should visit the site and meet you in person. The first meeting should cover:

LIST:Your brief and the place: how you want to use the garden, children or pets, and the style and colours of the house.|The space: entrances, boundaries, neighbours and features such as large trees, water points and windows, ideally in a rough sketch.|What lies beyond the garden, which helps decide what to hide or reveal, plus orientation, so you know where sun and shade fall, and topography: a sunken garden collects more water.|Wind, which can limit use and may call for trees chosen as windbreaks.|Borders and fences: height and material rules, and whether a fence should open a view or give security.|Drainage and irrigation, what exists and what is needed, and whether plant choice can manage water instead.|Slopes, which should be mapped and can be used to add interest.|Utilities: water, gas, electricity and sewage, which need access and should not lie under hard surfaces or large shrubs.|Soil: structure and pH decide what will thrive, and existing plants offer clues. Camellias struggle in heavy clay, for example, viburnums prefer alkaline soil, and conifers acidify soil, which suits rhododendrons but also encourages horsetail.

title: What’s Wrong with my Plants? Part 2
review: Technical advice, including a spray concentration. Needs horticultural review before being treated as current guidance.
excerpt: Spotting magnesium, calcium and iron shortages in garden plants.
body: Part two of a guide to reading plant nutrient problems, covering magnesium, lime (calcium) and iron.

Magnesium is part of chlorophyll and supports many enzymes. When it is short, lower leaves dry out, leaves lighten and their edges curl upward. Over time the edges turn red or brown while the veins stay green.

Calcium plays a basic role in soil pH. A shortage is often linked to too much magnesium or potassium, or to high soil acidity. Young leaves may change shape and curl at the edges, veins may turn light brown, roots weaken and fruit can develop dry spots.

Iron deficiency shows quickly in rhododendron, grapevine, hydrangea, box and surfinia. It usually follows poor air-water balance, low oxygen or too much lime (pH above 7.5), and the upper leaves turn yellowish-white with green veins.

It is hard to correct fully. The article recommends adjusting soil pH and watering with soft, lime-free water, which also loosens compacted soil. It says an iron chelate foliar spray at 0.1–0.2% can restore colour within about ten days.

title: What’s Wrong with my Plants? Part 1
review: Technical advice. Needs horticultural review before being treated as current guidance.
excerpt: Reading nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus shortages and excesses in garden plants.
body: Six elements matter most for healthy growth: nitrogen, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, calcium and iron. Part one covers the first three.

Nitrogen builds the green parts of a plant and matters most in the growing season. Too little brings slow, weak growth, yellowing and browning leaves, and stems that turn woody early. Too much gives oversized plants with dark, dense foliage, late flowers, and greater vulnerability to cold and fungal disease.

Potassium regulates water balance in plant cells and supports drought tolerance, disease resistance and frost hardiness. A shortage causes weak growth, late and pale flowers, yellow edges on older leaves that later brown and curl, a bluish-green tint, wilting and poor branching. An excess usually means salty soil, which makes plants wilt and dry out.
Phosphorus is vital for flowering and seed. A shortage means late, poor flowering, weak fruiting and bluish-green leaves with purple spots, and lower leaves may turn orange.

title: Slugs and Snails: the Gardener’s Nightmare
review: Mentions slug pellets and a nematode product. Product advice has not been reviewed since 2017.
excerpt: Why prevention beats cure, and which plants slugs love, dislike or ignore.
body: Left unchecked, these small, inconspicuous creatures can ruin a garden. The article mentions slug pellets and nematode treatment, but its main advice is to make the garden less attractive to them: prevention is better than cure.
Slugs eat voraciously and have favourites, including tagetes, salvia, calendula, sunflowers, stock, mint, campanula, lupins, delphiniums, chrysanthemums, hostas and violas.

To protect those, the article suggests planting lavender, allium, santolina, alchemilla, aquilegia, astilbe, pulmonaria, heuchera, hellebores or vinca around them, since slugs and snails dislike being near these.
A third group is described as slug-and-snail safe, neither repelling nor attracting them: dianthus, peony, gypsophila, phlox, saxifrage, euphorbia, geranium and ferns.

title: Go Organic
review: Pest-control and feeding advice from 2017; not reviewed since.
excerpt: Early-spring habits that keep insects in check without harsh chemicals.
body: Prevention works better than fighting insects later, so start in early spring while the beds are being prepared. Acting early can keep a garden healthy without harsh chemicals, which protects people, children and pets.

The article recommends gentle methods. Nematodes, microscopic organisms added to the soil regularly, help control slugs, ants, leatherjackets, vine weevils and chafer grubs. Companion planting is another: onions grown alongside carrots can deter the insects that attack carrots.

For weeds, check your soil type. Gardens with many conifers, azaleas and camellias often struggle with weeds that like acid soil, and liming each year can noticeably reduce some of them, horsetail among them.
Healthy plants resist disease better, so feeding matters. Natural options include seaweed for all plant types, iron to thicken and green lawns, and manure or potash for vegetables.

title: The Perfect Christmas Tree
review: Seasonal. The ordering and delivery service mentioned in the original needs confirming before it is offered again.
excerpt: A few useful tips for choosing and keeping a Christmas tree.
body: Choose a spot away from heating, which helps the tree stay fresh longer. Measure the route into the house, including doors, hallways and stairs, so the tree fits through. Then decide what you want: whether it sheds needles, its colour, and whether it is full or slim.
When buying, pick a freshly cut tree, since one cut just before purchase lasts longer. Choose a stand with a water reservoir and keep it topped up, which also extends the tree’s life.

title: Late Autumn Gardening Tips
review: Seasonal tips from 2016; broadly timeless, but not reviewed since.
excerpt: Lifting and storing tender perennials so they flower bigger next spring.
body: Preparing the garden for winter is worthwhile. Lifting some perennials and storing them over winter can mean bigger, brighter flowers the following spring.

To lift plants: cut them down shortly after the first frost; lift carefully with a fork to protect the roots; shake off excess soil and let them dry; pack roots or tubers in open wooden trays with nearly dry potting compost or sand; store the trays somewhere dry, cool and frost-free, such as a greenhouse or shed; and check regularly for rot, removing anything unhealthy.
Chrysanthemum roots may need a heated greenhouse and watering in mid to late winter to restart growth. Dahlia tubers should stay cool and dry all winter.

Suitable plants for lifting include dahlias, cannas, tuberous begonias, gladioli, pelargoniums and chrysanthemums. For large, sensitive plants that cannot be lifted, such as artichokes and agapanthus, cover the bed with a thick mulch before winter.

title: Buxus Diseases
review: Written before box tree moth became widespread and names no products. Needs specialist review before being treated as current guidance.
excerpt: Box is a favourite in English gardens, but it is prone to several diseases and pests.
body: Box (Buxus) is popular in English gardens but vulnerable to fungal diseases, pests and mites. Warm, wet weather encourages fungal problems.

Buxus blight shows as black leaf spots around April and May, with leaves dropping and the disease spreading to young twigs. Volutella blight turns leaves brown but leaves them attached, with pale pink fungus underneath, and often follows pruning or frost damage. Less common root diseases include buxus rust and several root rots.

Pests include box tree caterpillars, bright green and quick to strip leaves; buxus sucker, whose larvae curl shoots into spoon shapes; spider mite, which leaves silver stripes on older leaves; gall mite; mussel scale on old twigs; and leaf-mining gall midge.

The original advice is to treat each with a suitable targeted product at the right time of year and to prevent problems by keeping plants well fed and maintained, because weak plants are more prone to disease.

title: Making Good Use of Fallen Leaves
excerpt: Rake leaves onto beds and borders, or make leaf mould, a good soil improver.
body: Raking fallen leaves off lawns and onto beds and borders lets them break down into leaf mould, a nutrient-rich soil conditioner. Left on grass or beds, leaves block light and air, can attract slugs and snails, and encourage fungal disease.
Excess leaves can be composted, but keep leaf mould separate from a mixed compost heap, because layering leaves with other material makes a soggy mass that breaks down badly.

The most effective method is a small wire-netting enclosure, with layers of leaves about four inches deep separated by light covers of soil. It takes roughly a year, compared with six to eight months for a conventional heap.

title: Managing Soil Condition with Garden Lime
review: Advice on lime application from 2014; check against current guidance before relying on it.
excerpt: Garden lime reduces the acidity found in some soils.
body: Garden lime counteracts acid soil, helping plants take up nutrients and adding calcium. Soil pH runs from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral. Most soils fall between 4 and 9, and about 6 to 7 is ideal. If a soil reads around 5.5, lime can be added to raise it, and inexpensive test kits from garden centres give a reasonable estimate.

Lime can go on at any time of year, but autumn, before winter and the first frosts, gives the best results. Neutral soils generally need it every third year, while very acid soils may need it annually.

Use lime only where there is a clear need and never exceed the recommended rate. Spread it evenly, keep it off leaves and stems, and keep it away from lime-hating plants such as rhododendrons, azaleas, camellias and heather. The original refers readers to the RHS website for more.

title: Mulching
excerpt: Why a layer of leaf mould, bark, compost or manure is one of the most valuable things you can do.
body: Mulch is a protective layer spread over the soil above plant and shrub roots, using materials such as leaf mould, bark, garden compost or well-rotted manure. It is among the easiest and most valuable garden practices.

It slows moisture loss in hot weather, so plants need watering less often. Well-composted materials also enrich the soil: as they break down they add organic matter that loosens the soil, supports roots, helps water soak in and stay available, and feeds earthworms. A thick, complete layer can stop weed seedlings emerging, prevent erosion, cushion soil from heavy rain, even out soil temperature and give the garden a polished look.

Applied in late autumn, mulch helps keep soil temperatures steadier. For winter protection, loose materials such as straw, hay or pine boughs insulate without packing down, and reduce repeated freezing and thawing.

title: Planting Spring Flowering Bulbs
excerpt: Plant between September and December, before the first frost, for a colourful spring.
body: Planting spring bulbs between September and December, before the first winter frost, gives a colourful spring. Good choices include daffodils, tulips, crocuses, hyacinths, lily of the valley, bluebells, puschkinia and fritillarias.

Bulbs are easy and need only well-drained soil and some sunshine. As a rule, plant each at two to three times its own height, about two bulb-widths apart, pointed end up. Refill the hole, break up large clumps and firm the soil gently.

In pots, choose a container to suit the bulbs, cover a large drainage hole with a crock, and fill with general-purpose compost mixed with a handful of horticultural grit. Potted bulbs need more attention: keep the compost moist, wrap pots against hard frost and cover with chicken wire to stop animals digging them up.

title: Autumn Lawn Care
review: Seasonal advice from 2014; no products named.
excerpt: Help a lawn recover from summer and prepare for winter: leaves, aeration, feeding and reseeding.
body: Autumn is a good time to help a lawn recover from summer heat and drought and prepare it for winter.

Clear fallen leaves from the grass at least weekly through autumn, with a rake or blower; left in place they form a damp, rotting layer that harms the grass. Summer foot traffic compacts soil, so aerate with a garden fork, making holes in the top few inches so rain and air reach the roots.
After the last summer mowing, feed with an autumn fertiliser of balanced nutrients and slow-release nitrogen, following the product’s directions.
Reseed bare patches in autumn: prick the surface with a fork, rake to a level seedbed, scatter seed evenly, cover with a thin layer of compost, firm with the back of a spade and water regularly.
